result.question:
Produce an exhaustive, annotated content inventory of everything related to Saint Expedite (St. Expedite / San Espedito / Santo Expedito / Sant'Espedito / Saint Expédit), for the purpose of building a comprehensive wiki. Expedite is global — cover ALL of the following and flag what's contested:

1. HISTORY & LEGEND: The historical basis (or lack thereof) — the Roman soldier martyr of Melitene (Armenia), c. 303 AD, feast day April 19. The Acta Sanctorum entry. The famous folk-etymology legend about a crate marked "spedito" (dispatched) arriving at a convent (Paris? New Orleans? both — trace the story's variants and debunk/date it). Whether the Vatican ever removed him from the calendar.

2. ICONOGRAPHY: Roman legionary depiction; the cross reading HODIE ("today"); the crow/raven underfoot reading CRAS ("tomorrow"); palm of martyrdom; standard variations by region.

3. CATHOLIC DEVOTION BY COUNTRY: patron of urgent/just causes, speed, against procrastination, merchants, examinations, sailors. Coverage in Italy (Acireale Sicily, Turin), France, Germany (was popular), Brazil (Santo Expedito — huge, Rio churches, Nov as his month?), Chile, Argentina, Peru, Mexico, Spain, Réunion (Saint-Expédit shrines everywhere — very distinctive red roadside shrines), Philippines, USA.

4. NEW ORLEANS & HOODOO / FOLK MAGIC: the Our Lady of Guadalupe chapel statue; pound cake / Sara Lee offerings; the practice of publishing thank-you notices in newspapers; petition/working traditions; overlap with Voodoo and hoodoo; associations and syncretism.

5. RÉUNION ISLAND: the uniquely intense red-shrine cult, syncretism with Hindu/Tamil practice, ambivalent/dark reputation (curses as well as favors), official Church discomfort.

6. PRAYERS, NOVENAS, RITUALS: standard novena, the specific petition-and-thanks contract structure, offerings (red flowers, pound cake, coins, water), what devotees promise.

7. CONTROVERSY & SCHOLARSHIP: is he a "fake saint"/manufactured devotion? Academic folklore and religious-studies literature. Bollandist skepticism. Comparisons to other "commodity" or emergency saints (St. Jude, St. Rita).

8. MEDIA, MUSIC, CULTURE: songs, films, literature, place names, churches named for him, botánica/candle commerce.

For each area, annotate: what solid sources exist (scholarly vs devotional vs commercial), how reliable/contested the claims are, and which threads are messy or duplicative (the "sysop nightmare" of organizing this). Aim for a source-anchored map of the whole territory, not a polished essay.
result.summary: Saint Expedite (Expeditus / Espedito / Espédit) is a legendarily-attested early Christian martyr — "said to have been" a Roman soldier/centurion executed at Melitene (modern Malatya, Turkey) c. 303 AD during the Diocletianic Persecution, feast day 19 April — whose historicity is doubted by scholars but whose devotion is vigorously alive across three distinct centers of gravity. His standard iconography (Roman military dress, cross reading HODIE/"today", palm of martyrdom, crow underfoot reading CRAS/"tomorrow") makes him the saint of speed and against procrastination, which fuels a hoodoo/folk-magic commerce (Lucky Mojo product lines, pound-cake offerings) centered on New Orleans, and an intense, syncretic, ambivalent red-shrine cult on Réunion Island (340+ oratories, blended with Tamil/Hindu Kali worship, invoked for both favors and curses). The famous "crate marked expédit/expedite" folk-etymology exists in at least three documented variants (1781 Paris convent, New Orleans Our Lady of Guadalupe Chapel, and a Sicilian-immigrant chapel near Independence, Louisiana), all treated as apocryphal by scholarship. The controversy thread — whether he is a "manufactured" saint — is anchored by the documented fact that Pope Pius X acted against his cult/images in 1905, though the precise nature and date of any calendar removal is genuinely contested across sources. Réunion figures and the syncretism thesis rest on strong French academic sources; the crate legends and New Orleans voodoo syncretism rest on solid state-folklife documentation; the biographical "facts" are the weakest and most contested layer.

findings.claim: Expeditus is legendarily identified as a Roman soldier/centurion martyred at Melitene (modern Malatya, Turkey) c. April 303 AD during the Diocletianic Persecution, with a feast day of 19 April — but this identity is a tradition, not established history.
findings.evidence: Three sources converge on the 'said to have been' framing. Wikipedia: 'said to have been a Roman centurion in Armenia who was martyred around April 303 ... executed at Melitene ... commemorated by the Catholic Church on 19 April.' April 19 feast day is the strongest, uncontested element. Crucially, claims asserting hard biographical facts (that he definitively commanded the XII Fulminata Legion, died under Diocletian, etc.) were REFUTED in verification (0-3 votes) — the legion attribution and definitive existence are devotional embellishments, not established fact.

findings.claim: The 'crate' folk-etymology legend — a shipment marked 'spedito/expédit/expedite' (dispatched) mistaken for the saint's name — exists in at least three documented regional variants: a 1781 Paris convent, the New Orleans Our Lady of Guadalupe Chapel, and a Sicilian-immigrant chapel near Independence, Louisiana. All are treated as apocryphal.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia documents the 1781 Paris variant ('The senders had written expédit on the case ... The nuns assumed that Expédit was the name of a martyr') and the New Orleans variant ('a large shipment of statues ... labeled Expedite ... assumed that must be the saint's name'). The Louisiana Folklife Program (a state cultural-development body) documents a third, distinct Independence, LA / Sicilian-immigrant variant with its own chapel — while noting it is 'fairly new' and likely derivative of the more widespread New Orleans legend. Scholarship treats all as folk-etymology, not history.

findings.claim: Pope Pius X acted against Expeditus's cult in 1905 — striking his name from the list of martyrs and/or banning his images from churches — but the effort failed and the exact nature/date of any calendar removal is genuinely contested.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia (citing Mathew Kuefler, 'The Convertible Saint,' Journal of Religious History 42(1), 2016/2018): 'His name was struck off the list of martyrs by Pope Pius X in 1905, and his image was banned from churches, without success.' catholic.org repeats 'removed from the official list of martyrs by Pope Pius X in 1905.' BUT sources disagree on what the 1905 act actually was (removing unauthorized statues/images from Roman churches vs. deleting a martyrology entry); formal calendar suppression is elsewhere dated to the 1969/2001 revisions. This inconsistency is exactly why the detail is flagged as shaky. This is the core anchor of the 'manufactured/fake saint' controversy thread.
findings.vote: 3-0 (Pius X acted, effort failed); 2-1 (1905 removal flagged as contested)

findings.claim: The standard iconography depicts Expeditus in Roman military attire holding a cross inscribed HODIE ('today') and a palm of martyrdom, his right foot crushing a crow/raven from whose mouth issues CRAS ('tomorrow') — dramatizing the pun that resisting delay ('tomorrow') is a triumph of acting today.
findings.evidence: Four independent sources give the same type. Wikipedia: 'holding a cross, inscribed with the Latin word hodie (today). A banderole with the word cras (tomorrow) emerges from the crow's mouth.' catholic.org adds the legend gloss: 'the devil, appearing as a crow, tried to delay him by croaking Cras ... he crushed the bird underfoot, declaring Hodie!' Minor variant noted: some EARLY images showed a clock rather than the HODIE cross, but the mature/standard type is settled and uncontested.

findings.claim: In hoodoo/folk-magic, Saint Expedite is the patron of speed — invoked for rapid results, luck in a hurry, and an end to procrastination and delays — supported by an established commercial supply trade.
findings.evidence: Lucky Mojo Curio Co. (cat yronwode, a recognized hoodoo authority) sells a full Saint Expedite line: Dressing Oil ($10), Incense Powder ($8), Sachet Powder ($8), Bath Crystals ($8), and two vigil-candle tiers (Fixed $13, Set on Altar $35), framed 'For rapid results, luck in a hurry, an end to procrastination and delays.' Independently corroborated by multiple vendors and non-commercial blogs (Original Botanica, Lilith Dorsey/Patheos 'Patron Saint of Hurry Up'). This is the correct evidentiary base for a living folk tradition — practitioner/supplier consensus rather than doctrine.

findings.claim: In New Orleans, St. Expedite was syncretized into Louisiana Voodoo as a 'voodoo saint' fed pound cake (locally, Sara Lee) in exchange for granting favors; a statue in the Our Lady of Guadalupe Chapel near St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (Marie Laveau's burial site) receives such offerings to 'expedite' requests.
findings.evidence: Louisiana Folklife Program: 'St. Expedite became a revered voodoo saint who, in keeping with voodoo custom—one must feed the gods—asked to be given pound cake for granting favors.' Wikipedia (Louisiana Voodoo): 'Across the street from the cemetery where Laveau is buried, offerings of pound cake are left to the statue of Saint Expedite ... believed to expedite the favors asked of the Voodoo queen.' Caveat: scholars sometimes distinguish hoodoo (folk-magic) from Voodoo (religion) — the pound-cake practice may be more precisely hoodoo — and the chapel is ~one block from the cemetery, not literally across the street. Core practice is well-attested.

findings.claim: On Réunion Island, an intensely local red-shrine cult of Saint-Expédit emerged in the 1930s and grew explosively — from ~94–100 oratories in the 1970s to 337–338 oratories plus 31 chapels by the late 1990s (roughly one shrine per 2,000 inhabitants), sited at crossroads and increasingly on private property.
findings.evidence: Presses universitaires de Rennes (academic): first chapels attested in the 1930s; 94 oratories in 1970; 337 by 1997 (last known census). 7lameslamer.net: Philippe Reignier's 1998 census (his Université de La Réunion doctoral thesis, defended 2001) counted 338 oratoires + 31 chapelles across 250 sites, roughly quadrupling since Prosper Eve's 1977 baseline (~92+8). les-oratoires.asso.fr: 340+ today, first statue 1931 at Notre-Dame de la Délivrance (St-Denis), sited at crossroads and increasingly on private property. Figures may recycle the ~1997/1998 census as 'today' and exclude home shrines, making them a conservative floor.

findings.claim: The Réunion cult is an explicit case of syncretism with Malagasy and Tamil/Hindu practice: its blood-red color derives from the goddess Kali, some devotees abstain from meat or pray in Tamil, and he is venerated by Catholics, Hindus, and Malagasy alike.
findings.evidence: Presses universitaires de Rennes: 'Le rouge sang qui caractérise le culte de saint Expédit a été emprunté à la terrible déesse Kali' and devotees adopt Hindu rites, 'abstinence de viande ... ou même prières en tamoul.' 7lameslamer.net names 'le phénomène de syncrétisme ... à travers les greffes malgaches et indiennes.' les-oratoires: red is 'la couleur sacrée des pratiques malabares' (Tamil/Malabar). NOTE: a competing claim deriving the red from the saint's iconographic purple military cloak was REFUTED (0-3); the Kali/Malabar attribution is the supported one, though it remains scholarly-interpretive rather than proven.
findings.vote: 3-0 across three claims; cloak-origin alternative refuted 0-3

findings.claim: The Réunion Saint-Expédit has an ambivalent, feared, 'dark' reputation: invoked not only for healing, jobs, and exam success but also to eliminate rivals in love or business, and dreaded for swift retribution if vows go unpaid — a tension the official Church views with discomfort.
findings.evidence: Presses universitaires de Rennes states devotees invoke him 'pour se débarrasser d'un rival en amour ou en affaires' and that his vengeance is feared — 'One must pay him, and quickly!' Corroborated by multiple Réunion sources (linfo.re, saint-expedit.fr, reunion-tourisme.info) describing the same feared/ambivalent character. Caveat: a related claim that the Réunion diocese specifically removed him from the calendar in 1965 and that guides warn tourists away was REFUTED (1-2) — Church discomfort is real but that specific institutional detail did not survive verification.

result.caveats: Source strength is highly uneven across the territory — a genuine 'sysop nightmare.' (1) The BIOGRAPHICAL layer is the weakest and most contested: no reliable evidence establishes Expeditus existed; hard-fact claims (XII Fulminata legion command, definitive death under Diocletian, hundreds-of-thousands Latin American crowds) were all REFUTED 0-3 as devotional embellishment. Only the hedged 'said to have been' form survives. The Delehaye 'Elpidius misreading' / 'light-pack soldier' etymology thread is real scholarship but the specific claim about it split 1-2 and is not included as confirmed here. (2) The Pius X / 1905 REMOVAL detail is genuinely muddled: sources disagree whether it was images/statues or a martyrology entry, and formal calendar suppression is variously dated 1905, 1969, or 2001 — treat any single date with suspicion. (3) RÉUNION figures are strong (French academic + census) but the '340+' count likely recycles a ~1997/1998 census as 'current' and excludes private home shrines, so it is a floor, not a live count; the Kali color-origin is scholarly interpretation, not proven fact. (4) NEW ORLEANS/hoodoo claims rest appropriately on folklife documentation and practitioner/vendor consensus — correct for a living folk tradition, but the hoodoo-vs-Voodoo distinction is blurred in popular sources. (5) Commercial sources (Lucky Mojo, botánicas) are reliable only as evidence of what the trade sells and believes, not as historical authority. (6) Nearly all Réunion sourcing is French-language.
openQuestions: What is the precise, documented nature of Pope Pius X's 1905 action — a Congregation of Rites decree on images/statues in Roman churches, or an actual martyrology deletion — and when was Expeditus formally removed from (or retained in) the General Roman Calendar (1969 vs. 2001 revision)?

How large and organized is the Brazilian devotion (Santo Expedito) — Rio churches, an alleged November 'month,' crowd sizes? The hundreds-of-thousands crowd claim was refuted, leaving Brazilian coverage (a major part of the brief) thinly sourced and needing dedicated Portuguese-language research.

What is the current, post-2000 census of Réunion oratories, and how does the official Réunion diocese formally position itself toward the cult today (the specific 1965 calendar-removal claim did not survive verification)?

What primary scholarship exists on the German popularity of the devotion and its decline, and on the Italian centers (Acireale, Sicily; Turin) — these regions in the brief remain essentially unsourced in the verified claim set?

refuted.claim: Expeditus is traditionally identified as commander of the XII Fulminata Legion who died c. 303 AD in Melitene (modern Malatya, Turkey) under Emperor Diocletian.
His feast day is April 19, and devotion is especially strong in Latin America and Brazil, with crowds reaching into the hundreds of thousands.

The saint's historicity is contested: hagiographer Hippolyte Delehaye argued 'Expeditus' is a misreading of 'Elpidius', and the name is Latin for a lightly-equipped soldier, suggesting an anonymous individual known by profession.
St. Expeditus was a Roman centurion in the Legio XII Fulminata, martyred in Melitene during the Diocletianic Persecution around April 303 AD.

The Catholic Church does not officially recognize St. Expedito as a saint, yet many South Louisiana families remain strongly devoted to him — a data point for the 'manufactured/unrecognized devotion' controversy thread.
The distinctive red color of Réunion's Saint-Expédit shrines derives from the saint's iconographic purple military cloak (paludamentum).

The Réunion évêché (diocese) removed Saint Expédit from the calendar of Saints in 1965, distancing the official Church from the cult; tourist guides advise avoiding the oratories as associated with occult forces.
